rv.q: If it’s just a touch overstretched and undernourished, it is also, on the whole, very nicely done.
It’s not a radical or earthshaking show, but fans of stately period dramas with a feminist twinkle won’t go away disappointed.
Still, the play has a delicate emotional power that takes hold slowly and has a lovely, strong, central performance from Dulau.

As such, I cannot urge you enough to go and see this intense and powerful drama which is hugely entertaining and speaks volumes about the quality of the source material and those who have been charged with bringing it to life.
Bird Grove instead turns out to be a quietly scorching play about the price paid by a restless spirit who refuses to be reined-in.
That said, Bird Grove is more enjoyable in its tightly written, and often humorous, often ironic, first half than in its second, which does meander a bit.
Too often, oafish suitors, awkward dinners and hackneyed cries of “I want to read!” overwhelm the tender portrait of a complex domestic life that we see glimpses of throughout.
The performances are fine across the board, but the script is lacking in chances to shine.

cn.t: Campbell's elegantly written drama about young Mary Ann Evans before she became George Eliot receives mixed reviews. Critics praise the craftsmanship and performances, but question whether this origin story justifies itself beyond its famous subject.
